newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler denies it to cut 23,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Daimler denies it to cut 23,000 jobs.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG on Monday denied comments at the weekend from a top union leader that the German industrial group planned to cut some 23,000 jobs in the coming years.
Daimler said in a statement that it expected a stable employment situation in 1997 and saw no reason for major changes in its workforce in the coming years.
"Comments about plans to cut 23,000 jobs at Daimler-Benz are false," Daimler management board member Heiner Tropitzsch, who is responsible for personnel issues, said in a statement.
"There are no such plans," he said, noting the statements at the weekend were due to a "misunderstanding". "For the foreseeable coming years, we see no reason for this situation to change," he said.
Walter Riester, deputy head of the German metalworkers union IG Metall, said on Sunday in a newspaper interview that the 23,000 jobs would be cut by the turn of the century.

Riester also told the Berliner Zeitung that Daimler, maker of Mercedes vehicles and also a key player in the aerospace industry, planned to boost sales by 26 percent by 1999 but that its payroll would have to be cut by eight percent.
Tropitzsch said in the statement that Daimler stood by his statements at Daimler's annual news conference in early April at which he said the worst of Daimler's job cuts were over.
Daimler had at the end of 1996 about 290,000 employees around the world, about 21,000 less than at the end of 1995.
The cuts were mostly due to restructuring measures, which included disposing of troubled electronics group AEG and Dutch aircraft maker Fokker NV.
